title: Replying to @Beeptbeep #broadway #theatre  #theatretiktok #fyp
transcript: a couple people asked me to explain the concept of an in-person theatre lottery which makes me feel incredibly old because this used to be a huge pillar of Broadway fan culture but genuinely no shame to the people who asked because you're right like except for this one situation it's basically a thing of the past So for this episode of Overthinking Theatre Throwback let's do a little deep dive on Broadway lotteries so famously the tradition of the Broadway lottery started with RENT in 1996 as a way to manage demand that was too high for the first-come-first-served rush tickets (which RENT also invented) The practice caught on and over the next couple decades it became extremely common sometimes too common where they were kind of overestimating demand like one time I went to a lottery where so few people showed up that they just sold tickets to everyone who was there but most lotteries managed to draw a pretty decent crowd and essentially here's how it worked: usually 2.5 hours before each performance they'd begin taking entries you could show up and enter anytime within the next half hour and 2 hours before the show they begin selecting winners and it was fully analog it was done on the sidewalk in front of the theatre you would write down your name on a slip of paper and like with the digital lotteries you indicate if you want 1 or 2 tickets They’d be collected in a little metal spinner thing and then a human being would stick their hand in and select names at random until they ran out of allocated tickets some shows if they had a lot of unsold tickets that night would also offer a “lotto loser” deal for anyone who had lost the lottery they could get tickets that were maybe $10 or $20 more expensive and these lotteries were a big deal in the fan community there were different schools of thought on how to fold the paper there was superstition involved some people I knew had like their “lucky spot” [to stand in] it was also considered good etiquette to cheer and clap for every winner even if it wasn’t someone you knew there were also more strategic traditions of like if you only need one ticket for yourself you would pair up with a stranger who also only needed one ticket to double your chances friends would help each other out where you might show up to the lottery when you don't even wanna see the show just to help your friend increase their odds, and vice versa or even if your friend does want tickets for themselves you could still form a reciprocal alliance like let's say I arrive with Friend A but then I run into Friend B at the lottery if Friend A's name gets called and wins ticket for the two of us and then my name gets called after that I'd still claim the tickets and give them to Friend B and that could go on and on depending on how big the constellations of friends were and sometimes you'd be just communicating with eye contact and hand signals from across the crowd sometimes you'd see actors from the show sometimes other people in the industry probably the funniest thing was when they were calling names at School of Rock, I think it was, and we all heard “Todrick Hall!” and we were like “what?” and sure enough Todrick Hall walks up to claim his tickets and we're like “alright, good for you I guess!” of course Hamilton had their famous Ham4Ham shows where twice a week before the lottery Lin would come out with special guests and they’d do a prepared performance for the crowd and it would get pretty crazy I remember one time they announced over the megaphone that there were 1300 people who showed up on 46th Street to watch but then throughout the 2010s digital lotteries became more and more common and in person lotteries began to fade away Wicked was the last hold out on Broadway I think they only got rid of their in person lottery like a year and a half ago but really, the age of in-person lotteries had passed long before that now I think the Public Theatre are the only ones in the city who will still occasionally do an in person lottery which is what prompted this video nowadays digital lotteries are the norm and some of them have been reduced to kind of an empty stunt where the ticket prices have gone so high and the seat locations have gotten worse to the point where it's almost like a regular discounted ticket a far cry from the $20 dollar front row tickets to RENT and it's not just inflation Rush and lottery prices both spiked in a pretty short span of time I remember being appalled in 2011 when I heard that Spider Man was selling rush ticket for a whopping $40 just a few years later it was the standard and now it's a good deal there's a lot of disagreement about whether the rise of digital lotteries is good or bad it removes barriers in the sense of allowing more people to enter but it also adds barriers in the sense that in some cases your chances of winning become so minuscule that it ceases to feel like a viable discount opportunity in the same way that a Powerball lottery is not a viable paycheck obviously not that extreme, but you get what I'm saying so what do you think? do you think the replacement of in person lotteries is net good or net bad for Broadway fans? and if you used to do a lot of in person lotteries I'd love to hear your fun memories of it too
